lines.text:
Diagnosis and Repair — Inside a Mechanic's Workshop

A car is the most complex machine most people own — and the one they understand least. When something goes wrong, the mechanic's workshop is where diagnosis meets repair. Understanding the vocabulary of this environment is practical: it helps you describe problems accurately, understand estimates, and make informed decisions about your vehicle.

The workshop is organised around a lift — a hydraulic platform that raises the vehicle to working height. A creeper — a low, wheeled board — allows the mechanic to slide beneath the car. A toolbox contains the essential hand tools: a wrench for turning bolts, a screwdriver for screws, a socket set for recessed fasteners, pliers for gripping, a hammer for striking, a pry bar for leverage, a torque wrench for precise tightening, a multimeter for testing electrical circuits, and a drill for making holes.

Diagnostic equipment has transformed the trade. A diagnostic scanner plugs into the car's computer and reads error codes — identifying faults in the engine, transmission, brakes, suspension, exhaust, cooling system, fuel system, electrical system, steering, drivetrain, and AC system. What once required hours of physical inspection can now be identified in minutes.

The most common services follow a predictable list. An oil change replaces used motor oil and the oil filter — recommended every five to ten thousand kilometres. A tire rotation moves tyres between positions to ensure even wear. Brake repair replaces worn brake pads or resurfaces rotors. A tune up replaces spark plugs, the air filter, and adjusts engine timing. An alignment corrects the angle of the wheels. An inspection checks the vehicle's safety and roadworthiness. Bodywork repairs dents and scratches. A paint job restores the exterior finish.

Fluids keep a vehicle alive. Motor oil lubricates the engine. Coolant prevents overheating. Brake fluid transmits pressure from the pedal to the brake pads. Transmission fluid lubricates the gearbox. Grease protects moving joints. Each has a reservoir, a drain point, and a replacement schedule.

Small parts matter. A gasket seals the junction between two surfaces. A bolt and a nut fasten components together. A washer distributes pressure beneath a bolt head. A hose clamp secures a rubber hose to a fitting. A spark plug ignites the fuel-air mixture. A muffler reduces exhaust noise. An alternator generates electricity. A radiator dissipates engine heat. A battery stores electrical energy.

Specialised equipment fills the workshop. An air compressor powers pneumatic tools. A tire changer removes and mounts tyres. A balancer ensures the tyre's weight is evenly distributed. A welder joins metal. A grinder smooths rough edges. An oil drain catches used oil during changes.

When repairs exceed on-site capability, a tow truck brings the vehicle to a larger facility. An estimate — a written breakdown of parts, labour, and cost — is provided before work begins. The customer approves or negotiates.

The mechanic's skill is diagnostic reasoning — the ability to trace a symptom (a noise, a vibration, a warning light) back to its cause, and then to fix it efficiently. That reasoning is as intellectual as it is physical.

lines.text: Hi, my car has been making a strange rattling noise, especially when I accelerate.

lines.text: Let me put it on the lift and take a look. Could be the exhaust or the muffler. When did it start?

lines.text: I'll run the diagnostic scanner first. That'll tell us if it's the alternator, the spark plug, or something else.

lines.text: While you're at it, can you check the brakes? I've been hearing a squeaking sound too.

lines.text: 'Tell' + person: 'told me that...' 'Say' + (to person): 'said (to me) that...' Never *'said me.' Correct alternatives: 'The mechanic told me...' / 'The mechanic said to me...' / 'The mechanic said that...' The person is the direct object of 'tell' but follows 'to' with 'say.'

lines.text: Causative 'have': have + object + past participle = arrange for someone to do it: 'have my car repaired', 'have the oil changed', 'have the tyres rotated.' The past participle ('repaired', not *'repair') is essential. Compare: 'I had my car repaired' (someone did it) vs. 'I repaired my car' (I did it myself).

lines.text: 'Since' requires a perfect tense. Present continuous (*is making since) is incorrect with 'since.' Use present perfect continuous for ongoing situations: 'has been making since last week.' Present perfect simple also works: 'has made a strange noise since...' The action started in the past and continues to the present — this requires a perfect form.

lines.text: Subject-verb agreement: 'brakes' (plural noun) → 'work' (plural verb). 'The brake works' (singular) vs. 'The brakes work' (plural). After 'if' in an indirect question, the verb agrees with its subject: 'check if the brakes work', 'check if the engine runs.' Don't be confused by the distance between subject and verb.

lines.text: 'Fewer' + countable plural: 'fewer mechanics', 'fewer workshops.' 'Less' + uncountable: 'less experience', 'less training', 'less expertise.' Mechanics are countable people, so 'fewer' is correct. A useful test: if you can put a number before the noun ('five mechanics'), use 'fewer.'

lines.text: 'Bonnet' (BrE) = 'hood' (AmE) = the front cover over the engine. 'Boot' (BrE) = 'trunk' (AmE) = the storage space at the back. 'Windscreen' (BrE) = 'windshield' (AmE). 'Wing mirror' (BrE) = 'side mirror' (AmE). 'Number plate' (BrE) = 'license plate' (AmE).

lines.text: 'MOT' stands for Ministry of Transport (its original name). Every car over 3 years old needs an annual MOT. It checks brakes, lights, steering, tyres, exhaust emissions, and structural condition. You cannot legally drive without a valid MOT. The test costs around £55 (set by law).

lines.text: 'Garage' (BrE) can mean: the repair shop, or the building at home where you park your car. 'Workshop' = the working area where repairs happen. 'Dealership' = an authorised shop that sells and services one brand of car. 'Body shop' = repairs bodywork and paint damage.

lines.text: 'Estimate' = approximate cost (can change). 'Quote' = fixed price (should not change). Always ask: 'Can you give me a quote?' before authorising work. 'Labour' = the cost of the mechanic's time. 'Parts' = the cost of replacement components. Your bill shows both separately.
